doc.title: Al Tinney interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Segregation in the service and thoughts on civil rights
summary: The Army was segregated; he reflects that civil rights change cost black jobs and that time would have solved it.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Was the service pretty much segregated at that time?

Definitely at the time I was in it was segregated. But I didn’t know it. I mean to me I had always lived like this. But I lived in the ghetto neighborhood, I didn’t realize anything then. I don’t know where my mind was. None of this bothered me.
Well when you’re in it, and not observing it, I think it’s different. When people write about it later and make — maybe at the time it wasn’t a big deal it was just the way things were.

You had a few spokesmen in the race that knew what was going on or wasn’t happy with what was going on, and wanted to change it, you now, not realizing that in some instances they were putting people in jeopardy you see. Like they were taking — actually when they did that they — what do you call it — saturated the black teachers and stuff out of jobs because now anybody could come in and get those jobs you see. Before when you had — you understand where I’m coming from?
Yeah. They were actually black positions you might say. And these were gone. Anybody could take — like even just a janitor, now it was open to anyone.
I see what you mean. So by opening things up it was almost detrimental to some people.

That’s right in some cases. Although — and it’s funny that time, time is the essence of anything that happens. Like the phone calls. If you wait the time will develop its own self and that’s what should have happened but didn’t happen. See the pressure was being put on and these marches in Selma where the kids were trampled on and the water thing, and you know when all of this would have developed in a sense of time. I would say that
wouldn’t have been necessary. A great leader, a man who led them was killed by it, and so I really don’t understand why we won’t wait for that phone call.
